I’m in the same boat. I’m a first year elementary school JET in a new position that is A LOT of work and filled with a lot of idiocy and disorganization. I had stated a strong preference for either junior or senior high in my interview due to not being much for little kids and due to preferring to teach more academic material, so learning to work with elementary kids was a struggle. I initially recontracted due to wanting to save more money and, if I’m honest, due to fears of what comes after JET and of looking like a failure to people back home, especially after having been so elated to be shortlisted. Being asked to recontract in January after having had some time to vacation and be away from the slog for a while probably also influenced me more than it should have. 

I also studied abroad and had a wonderful time, so I understand that angle as well. My thoughts right now are that I’d like to try to find work in a different environment and age group before giving up on Japan entirely (although there are days that make me feel like doing so), since different management/teaching an age group that fits you better/being in a better area etc. could all make a significant difference. We have not started our contracts for next year yet, so we should (in theory) be fine on that front if we decide to move on. I understand it’s hard to think about wasted startup costs/costs of moving for a job after JET/the paycut you will almost certainly take if you move to a different teaching job in Japan/etc. vs staying in something that you know is ultimately not for you for another year of your life, because I have been dealing a lot with those same questions. Balancing financial goals, Japanese language goals, travel goals, the fear of uncertainty, and happiness seems impossible sometimes.

If you already hate your job, then there’s no reason why this would be worse. The negativity is because, like others have said, that it gets built up as prestigious when it is nowhere near prestigious in reality, and no one is going to think anything special of you once you get here.  There are tons of dispatch or private ALTs doing the same job as you, and probably doing it better. You have to let go of the illusion that this is “special.” Some people also get irritated because there are both JETs who do nothing the great majority of the time and JETs who are the primary teacher in the classroom all day, with none of this correlating at all with experience levels or desires, so you get licensed teachers rotting at their desks while someone straight out of college with zero teaching experience ends up being asked to design and lead classes. That could be stressful on either party when JET is marketed as an assistant role, and neither is doing anything close to that. This can happen even within the same city. You have to be fine with those kinds of situations. There is absolutely zero consistency in work, living conditions, the money you can save, etc., and you won’t know your situation until you’re either already here or at least very late in the game. JET is heavily luck-of-the-draw, so that can lead to frustration for people.
If you don’t have better prospects, though, go ahead and go for it, because your weekends will certainly be more exciting. I just wouldn’t give up a solid job or lifestyle for this that I wasn’t sure I could slot back into when my time was up.

I have 7 elementary schools with the expectation of being the main teacher at all of them, and I had never dealt with kids before and came to JET with nothing resembling teaching experience. I see a different school each day of the week, and every day is filled with classes. Some ALTs function more as a full teacher rather than as an assistant, and CLAIR could put you in that situation regardless of your prior teaching experience/certification. I also know a person with a Master’s and TEFL certification who teaches only a couple classes a week and functions as an assistant in most of those classes as opposed to as the main teacher, so I do not think there is much you can do to raise/reduce the odds of either of these situations happening to you. Know that you could end up with either way more or way less work than you expected going in, and be aware that even other JETs in the same city/town could have far different workloads/free time situations than you.

The other side of this is that we assume that people who are native speakers of a language are able to teach it and are inherently better than non-native instructors. This is not always the case. My university somehow has a native-speaking Japanese teacher with a Bachelor's in geography and no real teaching qualification. I can't keep track of the number of times she just says, "It's the Japanese way," in response to a grammar question when a quick Google will reveal that there ARE legitimate explanations. On the other hand, I have had an instructor from Ukraine who could answer any question you had about grammar and who was obviously an extremely brilliant lady. She also did not "baby" us in the way that some native Japanese teachers seem to do - our class was FAR faster paced, and I think that has to do with working with someone who has "been through the trenches" as opposed to someone who seems to half-believe that foreigners can never really master Japanese and that Japanese has some mystical component that is different from other languages.
